title: The Three Miss Kings
description: Published in 1883 and Cambridge's best-known novel: the story of three sisters, newly arrived in Melbourne from the country, who must make their way in the marriage market of the colonial city.
plot_or_argument: Elizabeth, Patty and Eleanor King, orphaned and poor, come to Melbourne and are taken up by a wealthy family; each sister faces a choice between an advantageous marriage and her own judgment, and the novel follows them through courtship, disappointment and eventual settlement.
historical_context: The 1880s, colonial Melbourne, the marriage market of the new city, and the debate on women's education in Australia.
literary_significance: The Three Miss Kings is the most accomplished Australian novel of the 1880s and a central text in the history of Australian women's writing: its picture of the marriage market in colonial Melbourne is exact and unsentimental, and its three heroines are among the first fully realised Australian women in fiction.

title: Thirty Years in Australia
description: Published in 1903 and Cambridge's memoir of her life as a clergy wife in colonial Victoria: a central record of the woman settler's experience of Australia.
plot_or_argument: Cambridge recalls the voyage out, the parishes of the Victorian bush, the parsonage life, the drought, the floods, the bishop's visit, the birth of her children and the slow transformation of the Englishwoman into an Australian.
historical_context: The 1870s-1900s, the colony of Victoria, the Anglican church in Australia, and the experience of the English emigrant.
literary_significance: Thirty Years in Australia is one of the finest memoirs of Empire by a woman and a key text in the history of Australian settlement: it is the fullest account we have of the daily life of an English parsonage family in colonial Victoria.

title: A Mere Chance
description: Published in 1882 and the first of Cambridge's colonial novels: the story of a young woman's first season in Melbourne, and of the chances and choices that decide her life.
plot_or_argument: Rachel Fetherston comes to Melbourne to stay with her wealthy relatives and is courted by two men, the steady and the brilliant; her choice is shaped by the expectations of her family and by the accidents of colonial life.
historical_context: The 1880s, colonial Melbourne society, the 'season' in the new city, and the position of the poor relation.
literary_significance: A Mere Chance is an early and perceptive Australian novel of the marriage market and a key text in the development of the colonial novel of manners.

title: The Retrospect
description: Published in 1912 and Cambridge's second memoir: a backward look at her English childhood, her literary life and the changes of a long life.
plot_or_argument: Cambridge recalls her Norfolk childhood, her reading, her marriage, her early authorship and the Australian years, and reflects on the religious and social changes of the century she had lived through.
historical_context: The 1910s, the Edwardian memoir, and the retrospect of the colonial generation.
literary_significance: The Retrospect is a valuable Victorian and Edwardian memoir and an important source for the history of English and Australian women's writing.

title: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan
description: Published posthumously in 1882 and the first English retelling of the Indian epics by an Indian writer: ballads drawn from the Mahabharata, the Ramayana and the Puranas.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'Savitri', the story of the wife who wins back her husband from Death; 'Lakshman', from the Ramayana; 'Jogadhya Uma'; 'The Royal Ascetic and the Hind'; 'Dhruva'; 'Buttoo'; and 'Sindhu', among others.
literary_form: Poetry collection (posthumous, with a memoir by Edmund Gosse)
historical_context: The 1870s, the Bengal Renaissance, the Sanskrit epics in English translation, and the colonial education of the Indian elite.
literary_significance: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan is the founding work of Indian-English poetry: it is the first collection in which an Indian writer retells the national epics in English verse, and its ballads made the Sanskrit stories available to English readers in a form they could recognise.

title: A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields
description: Published in 1876 and the first book by an Indian writer of translations from French poetry: versions of Hugo, Lamartine, Chénier, Béranger and a hundred other French poets.
plot_or_argument: The volume presents French lyric poetry from the fifteenth century to the 1870s in English verse translations, with the original French text facing the translation for many poems.
literary_form: Collection of translations from French poetry
historical_context: The 1870s, the Indian engagement with French literature, the Bengal Renaissance, and the Victorian culture of verse translation.
literary_significance: A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields is a remarkable document of colonial literary culture and the first substantial body of French poetry translated by an Indian writer; it was praised by Edmund Gosse, who wrote the memoir of Toru Dutt for her posthumous volume.

title: Le Journal de Mademoiselle d'Arvers
description: Published posthumously in 1879 and the first novel written in French by an Indian: the journal of a young Frenchwoman, written when Toru Dutt was seventeen.
plot_or_argument: The journal records the life of a French girl in a provincial household, her love for a young man, the opposition of her family and her death — a story of sensibility in the manner of the French roman intime.
historical_context: The 1870s, the French novel of the inner life, the colonial education of Indian women, and the tradition of the journal intime.
literary_significance: Le Journal de Mademoiselle d'Arvers is a unique document: the only French novel of the nineteenth century written by an Indian, and evidence of the cosmopolitan literary culture of the Bengal Renaissance.

title: Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands
description: Published in 1857 with a preface by W. H. Russell of The Times and one of the great Victorian autobiographies: the life of a Jamaican-Scottish woman who nursed through the Crimean War as an independent businesswoman.
plot_or_argument: Seacole recounts her childhood in Kingston, her travels to England, Cuba and Panama, her nursing during the cholera epidemic in Jamaica and Panama, her journey to the Crimea after the official nursing service refused her, her British Hotel at Balaklava and her work under fire at Sevastopol.
historical_context: The 1850s, the Crimean War, the nursing reform of Florence Nightingale, the colonial colour line in Britain, and the abolition of slavery in the British Empire (1833).
literary_significance: Wonderful Adventures is the founding text of black British autobiography and one of the most important first-hand accounts of the Crimean War: it records a black woman's professional life in the British Empire with humour and authority, and it is now central to the study of race, nursing and empire in Victorian Britain.

title: Letters from the Crimea and the Press Reports
description: Written in 1855-56 and published in The Times and other papers during the Crimean War: Seacole's first-hand reports of the siege of Sevastopol, the hospitals and the condition of the troops.
plot_or_argument: The letters describe the crossing to Balaklava, the building of the British Hotel, the wounded after the battles of the Tchernaya and Sevastopol, and the cholera and fever of the camp.
historical_context: The 1855-56, the siege of Sevastopol, the Crimean campaign, and the new role of the war correspondent and the newspaper reader at home.
literary_significance: Seacole's Crimean correspondence is among the earliest war reportage by a woman and a primary source for the history of the campaign; it documents the work of an independent black nurse at the front and is a central document of Victorian newspaper culture.

title: Roughing It in the Bush; or, Life in Canada
description: Published in 1852 and the classic English memoir of Canadian settlement: thirty sketches of the years the Moodies spent clearing a farm in the backwoods of Upper Canada.
plot_or_argument: Moodie records the voyage out, the first winter in the bush, the clearing of the land, the births of her children, the drunken neighbours, the fires and illness, and the slow discovery that the gentility she brought from England is useless in the Canadian woods.
historical_context: The 1830s-40s, the settlement of Upper Canada, the emigrant trade, and the English middle-class emigration after the Napoleonic wars.
literary_significance: Roughing It in the Bush is the central text of English-Canadian literature and one of the greatest Victorian accounts of emigration: it created the image of the Canadian backwoods in English writing, and it is a foundational document of the literature of the frontier and of women's settler experience.

title: Life in the Clearings versus the Bush
description: Published in 1853 as the companion to Roughing It in the Bush: the towns, villages and society of Upper Canada, and the institutions of the settled colony.
plot_or_argument: Moodie describes the towns of Belleville and Cobourg, the schools, churches, asylums and prisons, the temperance movement, the Indians of the region and the society of the cleared land, in a series of sketches that complete her picture of Canadian life.
historical_context: The 1850s, the settled districts of Upper Canada, the reform of the asylum and the prison, and the temperance campaign.
literary_significance: Life in the Clearings is a primary source for the social history of Upper Canada and a key text in the literature of colonial society; it is the indispensable companion to Roughing It in the Bush.

title: Mark Hurdlestone; or, The Gold Worshipper
description: Published in 1853 and Moodie's most ambitious novel: the story of a miser and his family in the English countryside, written in the sensation manner of the 1850s.
plot_or_argument: Mark Hurdlestone, a wealthy miser, destroys the happiness of his children and is murdered for his gold; the novel follows the fortunes of his son and daughter and the working out of the curse of the gold.
historical_context: The 1850s, the sensation novel, the English money-getting society, and the Canadian audience for English fiction.
literary_significance: Mark Hurdlestone is a significant Canadian novel of the 1850s and a key example of the colonial adaptation of the sensation mode; its picture of the gold worshipper anticipates the money novels of the later century.

title: Flora Lyndsay; or, Passages in the Life of an Emigrant
description: Published in 1854 and the fictional companion to Roughing It in the Bush: the story of an English family's emigration to Canada, told as a novel.
plot_or_argument: Flora Lyndsay, a gentlewoman, emigrates with her husband and children, survives the Atlantic crossing, the cholera and the first winter, and establishes a household in the Canadian bush.
historical_context: The 1830s, the emigrant ship, the cholera epidemics, and the settlement of Upper Canada.
literary_significance: Flora Lyndsay is a key text in the literature of Canadian emigration and one of the first novels to make the emigrant woman's experience its subject.

title: 'The Song of the Lower Classes'
description: Written in 1847-48 and published in the Northern Star: the most famous of all Chartist songs, sung at mass meetings across Britain.
plot_or_argument: The song sets the labour of the poor against the wealth of the privileged — 'we plough the fields, we till the soil, we're the lower classes' — and calls on the workers to claim their rights by the strength of their numbers.
literary_form: Chartist song (published in the Northern Star)
historical_context: The 1848, the Chartist petition, the Kennington Common meeting, and the revolutionary year in Europe.
literary_significance: 'The Song of the Lower Classes' is the central poem of the Chartist movement and one of the most effective political songs in English: it was sung by tens of thousands, and it is the essential literary document of the first mass working-class movement in history.

title: The Gold Harp
description: Written in Tothill Fields prison in 1848-49 and published in 1849: a Chartist romance of the fourteenth and the nineteenth centuries, in which a medieval gold harp passes into the hands of the modern workers.
plot_or_argument: The novel moves between the England of the Peasants' Revolt and the England of the Chartists, tracing the gold harp of the title as a symbol of the people's inheritance, and ends with a vision of the coming republic.
historical_context: The 1848-49, the Chartist convention, the prison writings of the leaders, and the revolutionary tradition from 1381 to 1848.
literary_significance: The Gold Harp is the most important Chartist novel and a key text in the history of English working-class fiction: it is the only full-length novel written in prison by a Chartist leader and one of the first to attempt a revolutionary historical narrative.

title: The Battle Day, and Other Poems
description: Published in 1851 after his release from prison: the collected Chartist poems, including 'The Battle Day', 'The Factory Slave', 'The Prisoner of the Tower' and the elegy on the Chartist dead.
plot_or_argument: The poems range from the songs of the mass meeting to the prison lyric and the elegy for the martyrs of the movement; their subject is the hope of the revolution and the cost of the defeat.
historical_context: The 1850, the collapse of the Chartist movement after 1848, and the prison literature of the political detainee.
literary_significance: The Battle Day is the central collection of Chartist poetry and the finest body of English political verse between Shelley and Morris: it preserves the songs of the movement and records the experience of the political prisoner.

title: Woman's Wrongs
description: Published in 1853 and Jones's contribution to the early feminist argument in England: a series of lectures on the wrongs of women under English law and in the industrial system.
plot_or_argument: Jones examines the position of women in the factory, the marriage law, the property law and the labour market, and argues that the emancipation of women is inseparable from the emancipation of labour.
historical_context: The 1850s, the women's movement after the 1857 Matrimonial Causes Act debates, and the Chartist tradition of rights.
literary_significance: Woman's Wrongs is a significant and unjustly neglected document of early English feminism and a key text in the history of the alliance between the labour and women's movements.

title: Carols from the Coal-Fields
description: Published in 1886 and the best selection of Skipsey's poems: lyrics of the pit, elegies for the killed miners, songs of the Northumbrian coast, and the ballads of poverty and self-education.
plot_or_argument: The collection includes 'The Collier's Lad', 'The Dead Miner', 'The Old Pitman', 'Golden Hair', 'The Lonely Death' and 'A Memory', and its subjects are the pit, the cottage, the sea and the dead.
historical_context: The 1880s, the northern coalfield, the mining disasters of the 1860s-80s, and the self-taught literary culture of the miners' institutes.
literary_significance: Carols from the Coal-Fields is the finest single volume of English miner poetry and a key text in the literature of the working class: it preserves the voice of the Northumbrian pitman and the elegy for the dead miner in a way that no middle-class writer could.

title: A Book of Miscellaneous Lyrics
description: Published in 1878 and Skipsey's major collection of lyrics: poems of the Northumbrian countryside, the sea, the cottage and the pit.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'The Haymakers', 'The Cranes', 'The Wreck', 'The Starling' and 'The Old Church', and moves between the natural world and the industrial one.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Northumbrian landscape, and the Victorian taste for the rural lyric.
literary_significance: A Book of Miscellaneous Lyrics contains some of the finest minor English poetry of the century and shows the range of working-class literary culture in the 1870s.

title: Songs from the Cradle
description: Published in 1867 and Skipsey's volume of poems on childhood, the family and the loss of children: simple songs in the manner of the nursery rhyme and the ballad.
plot_or_argument: The poems are lullabies, songs of the cradle and elegies for dead children, written in a plain ballad metre and with a directness that owes much to the Border ballads.
historical_context: The 1860s, the high infant mortality of the coalfield, and the Victorian poetry of the family.
literary_significance: Songs from the Cradle is a remarkable body of working-class poetry on childhood and bereavement, and a key text in the literature of the nineteenth-century family.

title: A Lyric Garland
description: Published in 1880 and a further selection of Skipsey's lyrics: the Northumbrian poems, the sea pieces and the pit elegies that made his name.
plot_or_argument: The volume includes poems on the fishing villages of the Northumberland coast, the pit disasters of the 1870s and the poet's own reading and self-education.
historical_context: The 1880s, the Northumbrian fishing and mining communities, and the provincial literary societies.
literary_significance: A Lyric Garland consolidates Skipsey's reputation as the leading working-class poet of the north and is a key text in the history of provincial literary culture.
